Unit K11.317 (K. XI 317). ENGLISH:
GALEN ON LEECHES, REVULSION, THE CUPPING-GLASS, AND INCISION AND SCARIFICATION. Some who hunt leeches shut them up and use them for many conditions. For these, once tamed, readily take hold of the flesh. Those newly caught must be kept for one day, with a little blood thrown in to them for nourishment; for in this way their venomous quality will be squeezed out. At the time of use, let the part that is to be leeched be first rubbed with natron and smeared over, or scratched with the nails, for so they will take hold more readily.

Unit K11.317-318 (K. XI 317–318). ENGLISH:
One must put them into lukewarm water, in a clean, wide vessel; then, taking them up with a sponge and cleaning off the slimy matter, we shall apply them with our hands. After they have fastened on, we pour warm oil over the part, so that it is not chilled. In the case of hands or feet, one must put the part itself into the water where the leeches are. If they should take hold only a little, one must snip off their tails; for as the blood pours out, they do not cease drawing until we sprinkle salt or ash upon their mouths. After they have fallen off, one must draw out the venomous matter with a cupping-glass; if not, one must foment with sponges. As for the bodies (of the bitten places), if there is slight oozing, cumin or flour is to be sprinkled on, and then it is to be bound up with wool together with a little oil (ἐρίῳ ἔλαιον βραχὺ κατειλικτέον). But if there should be a haemorrhage, linen cloths soaked in vinegar are to be applied, or burnt oak-gall, or one must soak a sponge in liquid pitch, burn it, and apply it. And one must know that leeches do not draw the blood that lies in the depth, but suck in that which lies next to the flesh.

Unit K11.318-319 (K. XI 318–319). ENGLISH:
We use them in place of cupping-glasses, and we pull them off whenever we judge that half the quantity of blood has been drawn. We check it and do not allow it to flow out until a sufficient amount has been separated off, since the part is cooled both by the leeches, which are cold by nature, and by the surrounding air. On revulsion. The most violent influxes of the humours we prevent, by means of revulsive remedies, from falling upon a part all at once. Revulsive remedies, in the case of an inclination towards the thorax and the belly, are those directed towards the hands; vomitings in the case of an inclination towards the lower parts, just as the revulsion by means of the sharper clysters is revulsive of that towards vomiting. Both of these inclinations, I mean those through the upper and the lower belly, you will divert by revulsion towards urines and sweats; and indeed the urines too towards sweats and evacuations of the belly. A revulsive remedy too is the cupping-glass applied beside the breasts. And with those pressed firmly upon the hypochondrium you will revulse the rush of blood towards the nostrils, just as also the immoderate flow through the womb.

Unit K11.319-320 (K. XI 319–320). ENGLISH:
Acrid drugs, too, applied to the kolpoi draw back by revulsion the inclinations of the humours toward the head and the viscera. And, in general, revulsion is to be performed, in the case of humours flowing upward, toward the parts below, and in the case of those flowing toward the parts below, the opposite; in the case of inward inclinations, outward, and again in the case of outward ones, inward; and if the flow inclines toward the right, toward the left, and if toward the left-hand side, toward the opposite parts. So too, the inclinations backward are to be drawn forward, and those toward the front, backward. On the cupping-glass. Cupping-glasses are useful after prior evacuation; for when patients are plethoric we shall not use them. By the same reasoning, in inflammations of the brain and the meninges too we shall not use cupping-glasses at the beginning of the affections, just as not in the case of any other inflamed part either, but when nothing is any longer flowing in and we have first evacuated the whole body, and there arises a need either to set in motion and lever out what is inflamed, or to draw it toward the outside. But while the affections are still coming on, the cupping-glass is to be applied not to the very limbs that are beginning to suffer, but to the parts continuous with them, for the sake of revulsion.

Unit K11.320-321 (K. XI 320–321). ENGLISH:
At the beginning, however, one must use repellents. The cupping-glass is able to evacuate the matter, to resolve pain, to diminish inflammation, to disperse flatulence, to restore the appetites, to make a slack stomach toned, to deliver from faintings, to transfer the fluxes from the deep parts and to dry them, and to check haemorrhages, and to draw off the corruptive powers of the menses, and to relieve the menses. On incision and scarification. We incise parts of the body which are either inflamed, or becoming scirrhous, or tense, or in a painful condition, or affected by flux, when the flux has already come to a standstill, or when acrid matter lies adjacent, or when a venomous power has fallen upon them from without, or when we wish to transfer the matter from certain parts to another. For example, we scarify the legs when the head is affected, or when we wish to diminish matter that is in excess in the body, and especially whenever the excess has arisen through the retention of matter which is habitually accustomed to be excreted.

Unit K11.321-322 (K. XI 321–322). ENGLISH:
For example, when haemorrhoids have been suppressed, we scarify the legs, having first bathed the patient, or fomenting (πυριᾷν) either in hot water or with a sponge. For I have not considered it suitable to open a vein many times in the year; for together with a great quantity of blood the vital pneuma is evacuated along with it, and when this is consumed too frequently, the whole bodily mass is chilled and all the psychic functions become worse. For this reason the removal should be made from the less important parts, such as the legs. Scarification also benefits eyes chronically affected by flux, conditions of the head, the affections about the chest and the back between the shoulders, and quinsies and impactions.
